zh.title: 之六 · 四十八条，三样东西
zh.deck: 名字从日常里借来；一个名字怎样用，不等于它已经把本性说清楚。

paragraphs: 第三部分讲情感。最后一条附释里，他回头清点：我认为，从欲望，快乐，悲伤这三种原始情感合出来的那些主要的情感和心神摇摆，我已经讲了。
又说：我说的只是主要的那些，不是可能有的一切心里的冲突。我相信，照前面讲的，人人都看得明白，情感一种跟一种合起来的方式那么多，由此生出来的变化那么多，没有哪个数目定得下来；可对我的用意来说，列出主要的就够了，我略去的其余那些，好奇的成分多过有用的。
到附释末尾，他说：关于情感的定义还有几处要注意，所以我在这里按次序把它们重说一遍，每一条该留意什么，插在中间。

sections.heading: 四十八条
paragraphs: 一是欲望，二是快乐，三是悲伤。快乐是人从较小的完满过渡到较大的完满，悲伤是人从较大的完满过渡到较小的完满。就这样往下排，排到第四十八条，其中许多条带着说明。第三条的说明，头一句是：我说过渡，因为快乐不是完满本身。
第四条是惊异。说明里他讲：我不把惊异算进情感里，也看不出有什么理由该算。讲到惊异，没有别的缘故，只因为习惯上，从三种原始情感派生出来的一些情感，对着我们惊异的东西时，另有名字；同一个理由，也让我把轻视的定义添了进来。第五条就是轻视，后面还附了一句：崇敬和鄙夷的定义我这里不列，因为就我所知，没有哪一种情感是从它们得名的。
第二十条后面，他把话挑明：我知道这些名字照平常的用法另有意思。可我的用意不在讲词的意思，在讲东西的本性，拿来指它们的词，平常的意思跟我要用的意思不至于全不相干。这一点，提醒一次就够了。到第三十一条，他又带了一句：情感的名字，我已经提醒过，看的是它们的用处，多过它们的本性。

sections.heading: 伯伯和舅舅
paragraphs: 同一个男人，他弟弟的孩子管他叫伯伯，他妹妹的孩子管他叫舅舅，他自己的孩子管他叫爸爸。
人还是那一个。叫什么，看是谁在叫。

sections.heading: 除了这三样
paragraphs: 第四十八条的说明写到末尾，他说：醋意和别的心神摇摆，定义我一概不提，一来它们是从已经定义过的情感合成的，二来它们大多没有名字；这说明过日子用，知道个大概就够了。
紧跟着他说：从我们讲过的那些情感的定义看得很清楚，它们全都出于欲望，快乐，或者悲伤，或者不如说，除了这三样，什么也没有；每一样平常都有好几个名字，因为关系不一样，从外面给的叫法不一样。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 这句话后面，他给叫作心灵的受动的那种情感，下了一条总的定义，三样装在一句话里。他在随后的说明里逐处交代用词，交代到定义末了那半句，第三部分也就完了：
这半句是我添上的，为的是在快乐和悲伤之外，把欲望的本性也说出来。

notes: 对应第三部分第五十九条命题附释末尾、情感定义3—5、20、31、48，以及末尾情感总定义。四十八是编号的条数，不等于穷尽了一切心里的变化。
伯伯、舅舅与爸爸是本系列的类比。说明段落的精确总数不影响这里对命名与定义的区分，故不把它作为论据。
zh.aside: 《SAE第一批判》开卷给自己立过几条写法，第四条是：比喻不承担定义；术语先用严谨的话定义，比喻只替已经定义了的东西作注。斯宾诺莎在这里管的是名字：讲本性的是定义，名字从平常的用法里借来，用来指出是哪一样。这是旁注，不是论证。

en.title: Forty-Eight Definitions, Three Affects
en.deck: The names come from ordinary life. The distinctions need not follow ordinary usage.

paragraphs: Near the end of Part III, Spinoza takes stock. He thinks he has explained the chief emotions and vacillations of mind arising from desire, joy and sadness.

Chief, not every possible conflict. Affects can combine in indefinitely many ways. He believes the preceding account lets readers see how further variations arise; enumerating them all would satisfy curiosity more than his purpose.
There are still points to note about the definitions. He will set them out again, in order, with explanations inserted where needed.

sections.heading: What the list includes
paragraphs: Desire comes first, then joy, then sadness. Joy is a person’s passage from a lesser to a greater perfection; sadness is the passage in the other direction. Spinoza pauses over the word passage. Joy is not perfection itself.
The list reaches forty-eight definitions, many with additional explanations. It is not simply a catalogue assigning familiar names to independently obvious feelings.

The fourth item is wonder. Spinoza says he does not count it as an affect in its own right. Why include it? Because ordinary usage gives some affects different names when the object is something that astonishes us. A similar reason leads him to include contempt. He omits other related definitions where, to his knowledge, no further affect takes its name from them.

After the twentieth definition, he states the principle openly. He knows that ordinary usage gives these names other meanings. He is concerned with the nature of things, not with explaining words; he borrows names whose usual senses are not wholly unrelated to his intended use. One warning should suffice.
At the thirty-first item, the warning briefly returns: the names of the affects have been chosen with ordinary usage in view, rather than as exact statements of their nature.

sections.heading: One man, several relations
paragraphs: A man is called one kind of uncle by his younger brother’s children and another by his sister’s children; his own children call him father. Chinese kinship vocabulary makes the difference audible.
The man has not changed into three people. What he is called depends on the relation from which someone addresses him.
A name may help identify what we mean without, on its own, defining its nature.

sections.heading: Nothing beyond those three
paragraphs: At the end of the forty-eighth explanation, Spinoza leaves jealousy and further vacillations of mind undefined. They combine affects already defined, and many have no names of their own. Ordinary practical life, he observes, often manages with a broad understanding.

Then he gathers the account together. The affects arise from desire, joy or sadness—or, rather, are nothing beyond these three. Each may receive several names according to different relations and external denominations.
The names multiply as the perspective changes. The explanatory account is trying to identify what those names have in common, not to reproduce a dictionary of everyday feeling.

sections.heading: At the end
paragraphs: After the list comes a general definition of an affect insofar as it is a passion of the mind. Spinoza explains its wording piece by piece.

The final clause includes desire alongside joy and sadness. His explanation ends by saying that he added that clause for this purpose. The part closes with a writer telling us why he put a particular phrase into his definition.

en.aside: The SAE First Critique assigns metaphors an illustrative rather than definitional task: define the term precisely, then let the image help explain it. Spinoza is dealing here with names rather than metaphors. Definitions concern natures; names are borrowed from use to identify what is under discussion. The resemblance leaves the difference intact.
notes: Locations: the end of III.59, the Definitions of the Affects—especially 3–5, 20, 31 and 48—and the general definition of an affect. Forty-eight is the numbered sequence, not a claim to have enumerated every possible feeling.
The kinship example is the essay’s illustration. The precise total of explanatory blocks is not required to distinguish names from definitions.
